issues.legal_issue: A benami defence supported by evidence from both sides remains governed by the trial courts’ factual assessment when the appellate court has found that the defence was proved and that finding is affirmed by the High Court.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed ownership of property purchased in her name and sought possession from her son.
The defendants pleaded that the property had been purchased in the plaintiff’s name with her husband’s funds and that he was its real owner.
Both sides presented oral and documentary evidence.
The first appellate court found that the defendants had proved the benami plea, and the High Court affirmed that factual finding.
issues.conclusion: The defendants had discharged the initial burden of proving the benami plea; because both sides had adduced evidence, the question of burden of proof paled into insignificance, and the concurrent factual finding was not open to interference in the civil appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The party pleading benami bears the initial burden of proof. Where both sides adduce evidence and the appellate court evaluates it and finds the plea proved, the burden question pales into insignificance; a concurrent factual finding of that kind is not to be reopened in a civil appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

rule.if: is_civil_appeal_from_concurrent_benami_finding and benami_defence_raised and both_sides_adduced_evidence and appellate_court_found_defence_proved

predicates.is_civil_appeal_from_concurrent_benami_f: The proceeding is a civil appeal challenging a factual finding about a benami defence that was affirmed by a further appellate court.
predicates.benami_defence_raised: The defendants asserted that property held in another person’s name was in fact owned by someone else.
predicates.both_sides_adduced_evidence: The parties presented evidence supporting their respective positions on the alleged benami ownership.
predicates.appellate_court_found_defence_proved: The appellate court assessed the evidence and found that the defendants had proved their benami defence.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges a concurrent finding that a benami defence was proved after both sides presented evidence, the finding stands.

issues.legal_issue: The prohibition on benami pleas does not prevent adjudication of a plea raised before the relevant commencement date in a proceeding that was already pending on that date.
material_facts: The possession suit was filed before the relevant provisions of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act came into force.
The defendants raised their benami defence before those provisions came into force.
The suit remained pending on the relevant commencement date.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not preclude the court from deciding the benami defence because it had been raised before the relevant commencement date in a proceeding then pending.
issues.legal_principle: Under R. Rajagopala Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan, Sections 4(1) and 4(2) do not shut out a benami plea already raised before 19 May 1988 in a proceeding pending on that date. Those provisions bar later pleas to the extent explained in that decision, but do not retrospectively extinguish a plea already raised in a pending proceeding. The Court also relied on Heirs of Vrajlal Ganatra v. Heirs of Parshottam S. Shah and Sankana Hali & Sankana Institute v. Kishori Lal Goenka, and noted that R. Rajagopala Reddy overruled Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare.

predicates.is_benami_proceeding: The proceeding involves a claim or defence that property held in one person’s name is beneficially owned by another.
predicates.proceeding_pending_at_relevant_commencem: The proceeding was still pending when the relevant prohibition on benami pleas came into force.
predicates.benami_plea_raised_before_relevant_comme: A party raised the benami claim or defence before that prohibition came into force.

issues.definition: A benami plea remains adjudicable when it was raised before the relevant prohibition came into force in a proceeding that was pending at that time.

issues.legal_issue: A decision permitting a benami plea under an express statutory exception in a later-filed suit does not undermine the rule governing pleas already raised in proceedings pending at the relevant commencement date.
material_facts: The later decision concerned a suit filed after the relevant commencement date and property purchased in the name of a wife.
That decision considered the statutory exception for purchases in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter and the associated rebuttable presumption.
The later decision also referred to exceptions concerning property held for the benefit of Hindu undivided family coparceners or under a fiduciary relationship.
issues.conclusion: Nand Kishore Mehra did not doubt or displace R. Rajagopala Reddy; the decisions govern distinct aspects of the Act, including its express exceptions.
issues.legal_principle: R. Rajagopala Reddy governs the effect of Sections 4(1) and 4(2) on benami pleas raised before the relevant commencement date. Nand Kishore Mehra v. Sushila Mehra concerned a later-filed suit and the exception in Section 3(2), under which a purchase in the name of a wife or unmarried daughter is excepted from Section 3(1), subject to a rebuttable statutory presumption. Section 4(3) separately provides exceptions for property held for the benefit of Hindu undivided family coparceners or in a fiduciary capacity. These exceptions do not show that Nand Kishore Mehra displaced R. Rajagopala Reddy.

predicates.is_benami_act_interpretation_case: The proceeding requires the court to determine how statutory restrictions on benami claims or defences apply.
predicates.later_decision_concerned_post_commenceme: The later decision concerned a suit filed after the relevant statutory restrictions came into force.
predicates.later_decision_applied_express_statutory: The later decision allowed consideration of a benami plea because an express exception to the statutory prohibition applied.

issues.definition: A later decision applying an express exception in a post-commencement suit does not displace a prior interpretation governing benami pleas raised earlier in pending proceedings.
